flashcards.q: What are the two distinct root causes of training-serving skew?
flashcards.a: 1) Definition drift -- training and serving implement the 'same' feature with subtly different logic (joins, nulls, timezones, window boundaries). 2) Point-in-time leakage -- a naive join uses a feature's current value instead of its value as-of the label's timestamp.

flashcards.q: What's the observable symptom of training-serving skew?
flashcards.a: Strong offline evaluation metrics (e.g. AUC) but degraded live performance, with no code change and no error or alert -- discovered only when someone compares distributions or business metrics slip.

flashcards.q: What does a point-in-time-correct (as-of) join do differently from a naive join?
flashcards.a: It reconstructs, for each training label at timestamp T, the feature value that was actually valid AS OF T -- not the feature's current/latest value -- preventing future information from leaking into training.

flashcards.q: What single architectural primitive does every feature store implement?
flashcards.a: One shared feature definition/transformation materialized into two stores: an offline store (historical, time-series, for training) and an online store (low-latency KV, for serving) -- so both paths read the same computed values.

flashcards.q: What does a feature store guarantee, and what does it NOT guarantee?
flashcards.a: Guarantees: same feature definition materialized into both stores. Does NOT guarantee: execution-context equivalence -- the batch job and the real-time read path still run through different query planners, timing, and failure semantics, leaving a residual skew risk.

flashcards.q: Which two internal systems first productized the feature-store pattern, and roughly when?
flashcards.a: Uber's Michelangelo Palette and Airbnb's Zipline, both mid-2010s -- the first well-documented systems solving skew structurally via one shared definition + offline/online materialization.

flashcards.q: Compare Feast, Tecton, and SageMaker Feature Store on ownership and cost model.
flashcards.a: Feast: open source, you own infra (Redis online + warehouse offline), ~$2-5K/mo all-in mid-scale + eng time. Tecton: managed, consumption-based, no published rates, strongest at real-time/streaming with built-in point-in-time backfills. SageMaker Feature Store: AWS pay-as-you-go, best when already deep in the SageMaker ecosystem.

flashcards.q: When is a feature store the wrong tool entirely?
flashcards.a: When the workload has no real-time serving path at all (pure batch scoring) -- there's only one feature computation path, so there's no skew risk for the online/offline split to fix, and the online store adds cost with zero benefit.

flashcards.q: An offline evaluation AUC is suspiciously high (0.94) for a hard problem domain. What's the first hypothesis?
flashcards.a: Point-in-time leakage -- the training join is likely using feature values not actually available at label time. Verify by manually reconstructing a few examples' true as-of feature values and comparing against what the training set used.

flashcards.q: What's the 'unified execution layer' critique of feature stores?
flashcards.a: A minority but live argument that feature stores fix definition-level skew but not execution-level skew, since features still move between different execution contexts (batch vs real-time) with different query planners and timing semantics -- the deeper fix being training and serving sharing one execution engine computing features inline at query time.

flashcards.q: Why can identical feature definitions still produce different results between batch materialization and online serving?
flashcards.a: Late-arriving or out-of-order events can be handled differently by a streaming/online path versus a batch backfill job even under the same logical transformation definition -- an execution-context difference, not a definition difference.

flashcards.q: What should you monitor continuously to catch skew before it becomes a silent production incident?
flashcards.a: Online/offline value parity for matched entity-timestamp pairs (alerting on divergence beyond expected materialization lag), and feature value distribution drift between what training data used and what's currently served in production.
